newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH ELECTION-PARTIES' POSITION ON EMU.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH ELECTION-PARTIES' POSITION ON EMU.

text.p: France holds the final round of a two-stage parliamentary election on June 1. The following is a summary of the main parties' positions on the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) on January 1, 1999:
CENTRE-RIGHT RPR/UDF COALITION
The ruling centre-right is committed to launching a single currency on time in 1999.

But though the outgoing government had insisted on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht Treaty, the party softened its position in the course of the campaign. Plans by Prime Minister Alain Juppe to step down and his likely replacement by National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin if the centre-right wins are seen as reinforcing this softer approach to EMU.
Seguin campaigned against the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 referendum, but has since said he respects the popular vote in favour of a single currency.
It has the following positions on EMU:
-- Meeting Maastricht

Ministers in the outgoing government had pledged to do whatever was needed to cut the deficit to three percent of gross domestic product this year to meet Maastricht criteria, and promised to continue reducing the budget gap in future years.
Seguin has said cutting the budget deficit "must not be achieved at a pace which prevents the resumption of growth."
-- Italian, Spanish, Portuguese membership

The centre-right wants as many countries as possible to join EMU in 1999, including Italy, Spain and Portugal, if they meet Maastricht criteria. Juppe said during the campaign the decision on which countries qualify for EMU will be political and historical, overriding considerations of the "nth decimal".
-- Role of the ECB/European economic government
The centre-right says it is committed to independence of the future European Central Bank but wants an "economic government" to co-ordinate economic policies inside the euro zone.
The outgoing government had earlier settled for an informal stability council, more acceptable to France's partners than an "economic government".
-- Strength of the euro
The outgoing government said it wanted a stable, credible euro. Centre-right politicians have warned against any overvaluation of the euro against the dollar.
-- EU "stability pact" limiting deficits after 1999

Juppe and others railed against the pact as first proposed by Germany in 1996, but agreed to it after securing a compromise that leaves some room for political judgement on when countries whose deficits overshoot should be fined.
Seguin said during the campaign he hoped the EMU "straitjacket" would be loosened after the euro was launched and support from the German public secured.
SOCIALIST PARTY
The Socialist Party negotiated the Maastricht Treaty under late president Francois Mitterrand, who along with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl laid the foundations for monetary union.

Though still committed to launching the euro in 1999, it has set conditions on this. Party leader Lionel Jospin said during the campaign these are not "take it or leave it" conditions but meant as the basis for discussion. It set the following conditions:
-- Meeting Maastricht
The party opposes a dogmatic interpretation of Maastricht criteria, says the treaty itself leaves leeway to take account of trends shown by a country towards meeting EMU entry targets.
Jospin has said the Socialists would not impose a new round of austerity just to fulfil a strict reading of Maastricht, but would instead negotiate a political agreement with Germany.
-- Italian, Spanish, Portuguese membership
Italy, Spain and Portugal must be in EMU from the start, and Britain too if it wants.
-- Role of European Central Bank
The Socialist Party wants an "economic government" alongside the future European Central Bank, but says it respects the independence of the bank.
-- Strength of the euro
Party manifesto says the euro must not be overvalued against the dollar and the yen.
-- EU stability pact

The Socialist Party manifesto calls for a "solidarity and growth pact" rather than an "austerity pact". Jospin has said he does not feel bound by the stability pact negotiated by the outgoing government.
COMMUNIST PARTY
The Communists want a fresh referendum on the single currency, calling the creation of the euro an "ultra-liberal political project".
NATIONAL FRONT
The extreme-right party is militantly opposed to the single currency and would halt progress toward further European integration of most kinds.
It wants a fresh referendum on the euro.
GREENS

The Greens favour a single currency but with conditions. They oppose European liberalism and deregulation, want to scrap the EU's "stability pact", and are seeking policies to promote job creation, social progress and environmental protection. The Greens broadly support further European integration.
